name: Gujarati
variety: Standard Gujarati (educated speech of central Gujarat: Ahmedabad, Vadodara)
sources: Cardona, George (1965). A Gujarati Reference Grammar. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press.
Cardona, George & Suthar, Babu (2003). Gujarati. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Mistry, P. J. (1997). Gujarati phonology. In Kaye, Alan S. (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa, vol. 2. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Pandit, Prabodh B. (1957). Nasalization, aspiration and murmur in Gujarati. Indian Linguistics 17, 165-172.
Fischer-Jørgensen, Eli (1967). Phonetic analysis of breathy (murmured) vowels in Gujarati. Indian Linguistics 28, 71-139.
Dave, Radhekant (1967). A formant analysis of the clear, nasalized and murmured vowels in Gujarati. Indian Linguistics 28, 1-30.
Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2012). The phonetics of contrastive phonation in Gujarati. Journal of Phonetics 40, 780-795.

Esposito, Christina M. & Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2012). Contrastive breathiness across consonants and vowels: a comparative study of Gujarati and White Hmong. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(2), 123-143.
Shih, Shu-hao (2018). On the existence of sonority-driven stress in Gujarati. Phonology 35, 327-364.
de Lacy, Paul (2006). Markedness: Reduction and Preservation in Phonology. Cambridge University Press.
Firth, J. R. (1957). Phonetic observations on Gujarati. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 20, 231-241.

Khan, Sameer ud Dowla (2016). The intonation of South Asian languages: towards a comparative analysis. Proceedings of Formal Approaches to South Asian Languages 6, 23-36 (areal intonation pattern only).
contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced
modal versus murmured (breathy) vowels ([baɾ] 'twelve' : [ba̤ɾ] 'outside'), beside breathy voiced consonants: one of very few languages with both
close-mid versus open-mid vowels /e/ : /ɛ/ and /o/ : /ɔ/, which the script does not distinguish
no vowel length contrast: the long and short i and u of the script are one phoneme each
geminate consonants, best treated as clusters of two identical segments
allophony: /dʒʱ/ is often [z] or [zʱ]; [z] also occurs in Persian and English loans
/ɖ ɖʱ/ are flaps [ɽ ɽʱ] between vowels and finally
/ɭ/ is a retroflex lateral flap and /ɳ/ a nasalised retroflex flap; neither occurs word-initially
murmured vowels go back to vowel plus /ɦ/ sequences, still written with હ (બહાર [ba̤ɾ], બહેન [bɛ̤n]); in spelling pronunciation the sequence [VɦV] can return

in breathy vowels the breathiness is spread over the vowel and strongest near its middle; after a breathy voiced stop it is concentrated at the vowel onset and stronger (Esposito & Khan 2012; Khan 2012)
the nasals [ɲ ŋ] occur only before homorganic stops
vowels are longer when nasalised and in final syllables
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(C)(C); clusters mainly in Sanskrit, Persian and English loans
phonotactics: the inherent vowel /ə/ is not pronounced word-finally
medial schwa is deleted in polysyllabic stems before a vowel-initial suffix (VCəC + V gives VCCV)
a breathy voiced consonant and a murmured vowel do not occur in the same syllable (Pandit 1957)

stress.rule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable (Shih 2018); older descriptions let it shift to a syllable with /a/ and away from /ə/ (Cardona 1965; de Lacy 2006), which Shih's measurements did not confirm.
stress.cues: vowel quality only: stressed vowels are more peripheral (F1); duration, intensity and F0 gave no clear evidence (Shih 2018)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: slight centralisation of unstressed vowels; schwa deletion in weak positions
rhythm.notes: Class and final lengthening are assumptions from the areal pattern; no measurement could be verified.

length.notes: Vowel duration is allophonic. No duration figures for geminates could be verified.

intonation.declarative: presumably the areal pattern: a rise on each content word phrase, low at its start and high at its end, and a final fall to low
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the wh-word, final fall
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases
intonation.notes: Only impressionistic descriptions exist (Firth 1957); the entries follow the pattern shared by the South Asian languages that have been studied instrumentally (Khan 2016).

tone.notes: No lexical tone. Early studies reported a slight F0 lowering at the onset of murmured vowels; Khan 2012 found no reliable F0 or intensity difference in connected speech.

phonation: murmured (breathy) vowels: higher H1-H2, H1-A1, H1-A2 and H1-A3, lower cepstral peak prominence and harmonics-to-noise ratio above 500 Hz, lower contact quotient; noise is strongest in the middle of the vowel (Khan 2012)
breathy voiced stops and affricates /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/, with breathiness early in the following vowel

problems: Murmured vowels do not exist: હ is always a separate voiceless [h] between two full vowels, so બહેન, બહાર, મહેનત are [bəheːn], [bʌhaːɾ], [məheːnʌt] for [bɛ̤n], [ba̤ɾ], [mɛ̤nət̪].

Stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable before schwa deletion, so it often lands on a schwa and keeps it: સરકાર [səɾˈʌkaːɾ], છોકરી [cʰoːkˈʌɾi], બોલવું [boːlˈʌʋũ], ભારત [bʰaːɾˈʌt] for [səɾkaɾ], [tʃʰokɾi], [bolʋũ], [bʱaɾət̪].
Nasalised /a/ is a nasalised schwa: આંખ [ʌ̃kʰ], પાંચ [pʌ̃c], માં [mʌ̃].
ળ is the retroflex rhotic flap phoneme (ફળ prints [pʰʌr.]), not a lateral, and so merges with the flap allophone of /ɖ/.
Only [eː] and [oː] exist: the open-mid vowels /ɛ ɔ/ cannot be produced from normal spelling.
Vowel length follows the spelling of i and u although length is not contrastive.
Breathy voiced stops and h come from the Hindi base table (voiced closure plus voiceless aspiration sample); intonation uses the generic tunes.
good: nasal vowels, the retroflex series and /ɳ/ are present
ઝ as [z] is an accepted pronunciation
equal length settings for stressed and unstressed syllables suit the weak stress

notes: /f/ is the usual realisation of /pʰ/ and /z/ is marginal. The stable murmured vowels are /ɛ̤ a̤ ɔ̤ ə̤/, from older schwa plus /ɦ/ plus vowel; murmured high vowels and murmured diphthongs are less stable and arise mostly in casual speech. Some dialects lack modal /ɛ ɔ/, and an 'educated' style can replace murmured vowels by modal ones. Dave 1967 contains a formant analysis of clear, nasalised and murmured vowels, but I could not verify its figures, so vowel_formants is left out, as is VOT.
